Solar basics

Grid-connected solar versus off-grid systems

The grid is the cheapest battery most homes will ever have. What that means for the economics of staying connected — and when off-grid genuinely wins.

Published 30 September 2026Updated 15 October 20267 min readSolvanta Energy editorial

Every solar conversation eventually reaches the romantic question: could we cut the cord entirely? The honest answer starts with understanding what the grid actually provides — and what replacing it really costs.

What the grid does for a solar household

A grid connection is an always-available, effectively infinite battery and generator combined. It absorbs everything you export, supplies everything you cannot generate, and never runs flat during a cloudy fortnight. That is why grid-connected solar is the standard design: the household buys capacity only for its average needs, because the grid handles the extremes — for a daily supply charge rather than a capital cost.

The spectrum from grid-tied to self-sufficient

Designs along the independence spectrum — rough shapes, not quotes
ConfigurationOvernight and cloudy daysCost and complexity
Grid-connected solar onlyThe grid supplies everything the sun does notLowest cost; simplest; no outage protection
Solar + battery, grid backupBattery covers evenings; the grid covers winter and gloomModest step up; storage sized for evening load; partial outage backup possible
Grid-optional hybridBattery plus grid with engineered backup circuits; can ride through outagesHigher equipment spec; backup wiring throughout; still grid-supported in deep winter
Off-gridLarge battery plus oversized array or generator; weeks of autonomy must be designed inHighest cost by a wide margin; specialist design, maintenance and discipline required

Why off-grid costs so much more: the winter fortnight

An off-grid system must be sized not for the average day, but for the worst realistic stretch — days of heavy cloud in the shortest, darkest weeks of the year, carrying the household's full load with no grid to lean on. That single design requirement multiplies both array size and battery capacity, and usually still demands a backup generator or a deeply conservative lifestyle. The sizing difference between an average day and the worst fortnight is where off-grid economics are made or broken.

Professional off-grid design also adds obligations that grid-connected owners never think about: battery maintenance and replacement budgets, inverter redundancy, generator servicing, and the discipline to run heavy loads when energy is available rather than when convenient.

When off-grid genuinely makes sense

  • The property is remote enough that a grid connection quote is itself a large capital project — sometimes tens of thousands of dollars for poles, transformers and trenching.
  • The site is temporary or the connection is genuinely impossible under current rules.
  • The household genuinely accepts the discipline: appliance scheduling, winter conservatism, and maintenance as a way of life.
  • There is a specialist designer involved — off-grid is a systems-engineering project, not a bigger version of a rooftop job.

The honest middle ground

Most households drawn to 'independence' are actually looking for two things the grid-plus-battery middle provides at a fraction of the cost: protection from outages, and a smaller bill. A well-designed battery system with backup circuits delivers both, keeps the grid as the winter safety net, and avoids paying for the worst-case autonomy that off-grid demands. That is why the middle of the spectrum is where most genuinely happy households land.

Key takeaways

  • The grid is a near-infinite battery at a daily supply charge — expensive to replace with hardware.
  • Off-grid systems are sized for the worst fortnight, not the average day; that is the cost driver.
  • Grid plus battery delivers the two things most households actually want: outage cover and bill reduction.
  • Off-grid fits remote sites where connection cost is extreme — and households ready for its maintenance realities.
  • Independence is a spectrum with sensible stops in the middle.
